utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We're going to resume now. Let me say good morning to the interpreters, even if I don't see them very clearly from where I am sitting. I hope that everybody can hear me, everybody is on the right channel. I am on Channel 5. I see the Prosecution is ready, the Defence is ready, everybody is ready. All right. We can now resume. Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, I was just getting ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you can begin. That is, as soon as the witness comes in. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, good morning, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel. Good morning, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A bit too loud says the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A bit louder, a bit louder, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think you have a little button that you can use on the right-hand side of the equipment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that okay, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Examined by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, yesterday we finished the day talking about a series of orders, one of which came from the accused, Colonel Blaskic, on the 12th of April, concerning a list of HV officers that were in units in Central Bosnia. Now, before we move back to that order, let me ask you a question, as a follow-up question, from the November order -- excuse me, the October order, where General Blaskic again asked for information concerning HV units. And let me ask you, were there units and HV officers in other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina working with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The order that you mentioned from the month of October, could I see it? So as to be able to give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, sir. That's Exhibit 406 subdivision 26. While we're at it, 406/31 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: While that's being obtained, Mr. President, perhaps counsel could be more specific with respect to the term "other areas."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sure. We'll just give him a chance to take a look at the exhibits and then we'll go back to that question. No problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just by way of review, Brigadier, Exhibit 406/26 is an order signed by the accused or from the accused, I believe, it's a packet that we talked about yesterday -- yes, it is, of the 5th of October, 1992, where he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You said, "signed by the accused," I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand. I have a document here signed by Mr. Covic; is that the exhibit you're referring to, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Or maybe it's an error in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I was moving chronologically, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Fine. Perhaps the usher should stay next to the witness to help him with the order of the documents and then we can proceed more quickly. So you're starting with the order of the 5th of October; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I correct any impression, Mr. President, that this was a packet communication as the witness testified yesterday and the original packet in BSC has no signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This particular order on the 5th of October from the accused, asked for an urgent submission of data concerning HV officers in the unit. Now, you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said yesterday with regard to this document, if it was at all created in the command of the Operative Zone because I see no stamp or signature, it is just an assumption that it was drafted in the command of the Operative Zone. I can't allege that it was or was not because at the time I was not in the command of the Operative Zone. I said in my introduction that I joined the command of the Operative Zone on the 1st of November, 1992, so that I am not familiar with the contents of this order and I cannot claim that this is an order issued by the Commander of the Operative Zone. It is possible that it may have been created as the Prosecutor said, but I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But this is a question of principle, Brigadier. It's the absence of the stamp that leads you to believe that the order was not issued. I wish to draw your attention to the fact that this question could be raised for all the other orders tendered by the Defence. I am just drawing your attention to the problem. I am closing the brackets there. We have all been discussing orders that are photocopies, so let us be very careful. Your answer has been registered that because you see no stamp, that, perhaps, this order was not issued and that has been entered in the record. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may? I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Be very specific in your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When this document was made, I was not working in the command of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That I understood very well. That's another answer. You also said that there is no stamp and as a result you have dealt as to whether that order is issued. So there are two answers: Either you say, I was not active at the time and I can say nothing about this order which is an acceptable order, or you can say a stamp is missing. So it is possible that such an order was not issued, so that is quite a different answer. Thereby, you're opening the way for challenging all the orders that have been shown in the case, in this trial, and I am drawing your attention to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, I had no duties in the command of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but that is an answer I understood very well. I am talking about the stamp now. There is a very big problem regarding all the orders, those shown by the Prosecution, as well as those shown by the Defence. The Judges will want to know at a certain point, the authenticity of those orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps there is a translation issue, Mr. President. It's very clear to me what the witness is saying. He is saying that unlike the other orders, at least the book of them, that both the Prosecutor has shown him and the Defence, which he is able to identify with respect to this document. He neither recognises a signature, nor the seal of the Operative Zone, nor a packet communication stamp, nor does he have personal knowledge of the events because he wasn't working in the Operative Zone at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I wish to close the parenthesis, please continue with your questions, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, the next document that we were talking about yesterday at the close of the day was a document dated 26th November, 1992 and that is Document 406/31, which was a document that was signed by Zoran Covic, wherein he said at Point 3: "HV Croatian army members present in the region and wearing HV insignia must be warned to take them off as this creates trouble for the Republic of Croatia." Do you see that document, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see it and I see the point that you have just cited from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is: Were HVO officers -- excuse me, I apologise, HV officers and HV soldiers working and fighting with the HVO in other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina, such as Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say with certainty regarding the command of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. As regards official information about the participation of Croatian army officers in other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I cannot confirm that, but I have heard from reports from the media during the fighting around Dubrovnik that the Croatian army participated in the organisation of the defence, but I cannot confirm that because I have no official information. I wish also to add that throughout the war from '92 until '94 until the Washington Agreement, I had no occasion to leave the area which was surrounded at the time, so I cannot claim with certainty that that is true or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, you are now an officer in the federation army and you have been in continuous military service for how many years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the moment I joined the HVO I was never outside the service, which means since 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, since 1992, did you talk to other members of the HVO about the presence of HV officers and soldiers in Bosnia fighting and working with the HVO? Did you have any such conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, officially and formally, the participation of the Croatian army in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina following the Washington Agreement and the Split Agreement, the participation of the Croatian army in the final operations for the liberation of Bosnia-Herzegovina did exist and I had a certain duty within that framework and I am aware of that officially and formally. As for everything else, what happened in 1992 and 1993, I have no official information about that. But as I have said on the basis of information published by the media on the fighting in the area of Dubrovnik, Ravno, those reports said that the Croatian army was there, together with the HVO, fighting against the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, maybe my question wasn't clear. Let me be very precise. Did you have any conversations, official or unofficial, with any member of the HVO wherein you, Brigadier, discussed the presence of HV officers and HV soldiers fighting and working with the HVO in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please tell me exactly what time frame you're referring to? I told you about the period that I know about. Are you talking about '92/'93/'94?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am talking about the time frame 1992 and 1993. That time frame. Until the Washington Accord in the end of February, beginning of March, 1994. Did you have any such conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have never spoken about that to anyone, officially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about unofficially, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unofficially, also I cannot remember exactly when, how, where, because conversations among soldiers in the war can vary and I really cannot say with certainty anything that I cannot prove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, did you have any conversation among your soldier friends in the HVO about the presence of HV soldiers working and fighting with HVO soldiers in the Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have said very clearly, I know the area, the hinterland of Dubrovnik, the area of the village of Ravno, and I know that there were certain joint activities between HVO units and HV army units. As for fighting around Mostar and in other places, I really have no information and I cannot say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe we'll show the witness Exhibit 406/36. This document dated September, 1992 -- I'm sorry, this document should be dated 9 December, 1992. Let me read some portions from this to you, Brigadier. It is from the Mostar municipal headquarters, 9 December, 1992 and notes: "In regards to the strictly confidential order concerning self-eastern" -- excuse me, "In regards to the strictly confidential order concerning self-eastern Herzegovina Operative Zone Number 01286/1514 of 27 November, 1992, regarding various insignia and symbols on HVO unit uniforms, worn as opposed to the symbols stipulated by the decree on Herceg-Bosna armed forces which, as such, compromised the reputation of HVO and HV members by implying ideas which the world media may interpret as fascistic, I hereby order: 1. Commanders of a Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna HVO to ensure that unit members wear only HVO insignia and remove all other emblems." We're going to move down to three, Brigadier. I would gladly read the rest of it, but we'll move to three for the purpose to expedite matters. 3. "Wearing HVO insignia is linked to accusations against the Republic Croatian community and the Croatian community of Herzeg-Bosna regarding a direct deployment of HVO units in the territory of the Croatian community of Herzeg-Bosna, asked HV members with explanation to wear HV insignia during their deployment in our area." You can take a moment or two to read the rest of it. It goes on to a couple of more paragraphs, some of which is not legible. It is signed by Ivan Primorac, who is the 3rd HVO Brigade commander. Now Primorac's order indicates that HV members were deployed to the, at least to the Mostar area, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen this order before. This order, as can be seen, was drafted in the command of the Operative Zone of south-eastern Herzegovina. This command issued the order to its subordinate units, among which was the 3rd HVO Brigade. I really don't know anything about that Brigade, so I cannot say why such a document was drafted, except for what I said regarding the document we received in the command of the Operative Zone, which I explained yesterday and that is that soldiers who had fought in Croatia until the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and who had lived before the war in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, after the war started in Bosnia-Herzegovina, they came to Bosnia-Herzegovina wearing the uniforms and insignia of the Croatian army. As the desire of those soldiers was to keep those insignia, indicating membership, not only in the Croatian army, but in a particular unit of the Croatian army, such an order had to be issued to eliminate this. I don't know the specific figures, but I know that after the aggression against the Republic of Croatia, Croats, as well as Muslims and Bosniaks from the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who had been in the JNA service in Croatia at that moment, joined the Croatian army. A number of senior officers from Bosnia-Herzegovina were, at the beginning, officers of the Croatian army. When the JNA started the war against Bosnia-Herzegovina, they reported to the authorities of that republic and joined their forces. That is as much as I know about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, in this particular order, Mr. Primorac does indicate that there are HV members deployed to the Mostar area, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, objection to the form of the question. The witness said he wasn't there. The document speaks for itself as to what's in it. The form of the question is inappropriate. He is cross-examining the witness about something he doesn't have any knowledge about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am simply asking the witness whether or not he agrees that this particular order that says HV units are deployed to the Mostar area. Why, that's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We can all see what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I think, Mr. Kehoe, that Mr. Hayman is right. What do you want the witness to talk about this document? We have the document before us. It is signed by Mr. Primorac. There is nothing more to ask him. We're wasting time. I think we should speed up a little bit. I think that the witness has answered regarding the whole problem of the presence of the HV. He said that they were Bosniaks who went and came back wearing those uniforms, so let us speed up things a little, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, when did you take your position in Mostar that you currently hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the decision was taken on the organisation of the federation army, signed by a member of the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, and a member of the presidency, Kresimir Zubac, the decision defined that the army of the federation should consist of four corps. One of those corps is called the 1st Guards' Corps and it comprises all the units of the HVO. The other three corps comprise all the units of the former structure of the BH army. In addition to these corps, this decision also envisages certain additional units, such as a rapid deployment brigade, an artillery brigade and some other minor units which I can't recall just now. After this decision was taken on the 17th of March, 1996, I was appointed chief of staff of the 1st Army Corps of the federation army with a command post in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went to Mostar to take your position on the 17th of March, 1996; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet Mr. Primorac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the area of Mostar, there are several persons called Primorac, it is a frequent surname, so I don't know who this gentleman is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apparently he was the commander of the 3rd HVO Brigade in Mostar, and his first name is Ivan Primorac; did you meet that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ivan Primorac, as far as I can recall; but I'm absolutely not sure, but I do wish to answer your question, to the best of my recollection. For a time he was in the command of the military district of Mostar, but whether that is key, I'm really not sure. I would be glad to answer your question, but I do wish to avoid any guesswork.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since March of 1996, is it your testimony, since you've been stationed in Mostar in March of 1996, is it your testimony you have had no conversations, either official or unofficial, with any HVO members concerning the deployment of HV troops and officers in the Mostar area? Is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may correct you, from the 17th of March 1996 we did not go to Mostar on that very day. I first went to Posusje to take up my new duties, because we were based there; and it was only toward the end of September, I can't exactly remember the date, we moved to the barracks at the Heliodrom in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question remains the same. Since you were stationed in the barracks in the Heliodrom in September of 1996 until today, is it your testimony you haven't had any conversations, either official or unofficial, with any HVO people concerning the deployment of HV officers and soldiers in the Mostar area in '92 and '93? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Officially, no, but conversations, any particular conversations about this subject, I didn't have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, your testimony is you had neither official or unofficial conversations about this subject; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn back to the order that we discussed yesterday from the accused, where he asks for a list of HV officers in the units and I'm talking about Exhibit 406/55, which is also contained in 456/19, and that is the order of the 12th of April 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 406/55 as the transcript says, or is it 456, 406/55 or 456?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can use 406/55, that will suffice. INTERPRETER: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's the same document, so if we can use 406/55, that will be fine. It should be the order of the 12th of April 1993. Brigadier, this is the order that we were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, this is the order we were talking about yesterday, and I want to ask you a couple of follow-up questions here. Tell me, in number 2 it says, "Include in this list..." Blaskic asks for the name, the father's name, last name, number of the order with which he was sent to the HVO, his rank and the number of the transfer decree. What is this transfer decree and who issues this transfer decree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you asking me in principle, in the armed forces, or are you asking me specifically for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking what this order means, Brigadier, where it says that they want the number of a transfer decree. Is this a transfer decree that is signed by the HV to the HVO, sending a particular officer to a particular location in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that what we are talking about here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not have an opportunity to see these documents on transfers, because I did not work in personnel; however, in any army, if it is properly organised, in order to transfer any officer to any post, he has to have an order of transfer by the authorised officers. His authority is defined by the rules of these armed forces. Again, let me repeat to you, as I did not work on personnel issues, I never handled any such document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, would such a transfer decree be issued by the HV, transferring this soldier or this officer to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know whether such an order could be, or could have been issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this particular transfer decree obviously must have some type of number to it, some type of number, just as many of the documents you've discussed; because in the front-line it asks for a listing of the number of the order which he was sent to the HVO, in addition to the number of the transfer decree; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only guess in that respect. I said that I did not see such orders. I do not know their contents and I don't know under what circumstances, that is, if such orders had been issued. I'm not aware with which type of documents such a person would arrive at a new post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree with me, would you not, Brigadier, that this is pretty organised. They were asking for actually two particular documents, a number of an order to which he was sent to the HVO, and a number of the actual transfer decree. So, there are two documents concerning these particular officers which are discussed in this number 2; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies, you're mentioning two officers?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two documents, I apologise if I misspoke. Number 2 is talking about two particular documents, an order, from which he was sent to the HVO, and a transfer decree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, when we spoke about this document yesterday I said that as far as I recall this document was drafted on the basis of an order of the Chief of Staff of the main headquarters. Probably the person who wrote this, Ljubomir Jurcic, and Mrs. Stefica was the typist, I believe that he has no military training, and so he did not refer to the document on the basis of which this document was drafted, and he just copied down whatever the main headquarters of the HVO asked him to do. I don't know why the main headquarters of the HVO was looking for these particular names. I don't know the reasons for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you noted to us yesterday that as far as you knew there were no HV officers in Central Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said that, and I say that now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were HVO officers sent to Central Bosnia to consult with then, Colonel Blaskic, and other members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know of that. I did not meet such officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether or not you met them, did you ever discuss the fact that they were there with Blaskic and other members of the Central Bosnian Operative Zone staff?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: There are some mistakes in the transcript. You said, "were HVO officers sent to Central Bosnia to consult with Colonel Blaskic."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It should be HV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We have to be clear. Before they refer to the HV as HJ officers. The transcript has to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask again that question, given the correction in the transcript. Were HV officers sent to Central Bosnia to consult with Colonel Blaskic and other members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I did not know this. I personally did not meet the HV officers in the territory of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, whether or not you met them, if they were there, given your position in the headquarters, would you know about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I need not know any single case, because there are different areas that are covered, logistics, operations, and so on and so forth. So, if they had been there on some task regarding operations, then I would have known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, perhaps we shouldn't go too much round and round here. I think that the witness has told you everything that he knows about the question. Although he was at a high level, next to the accused, he was not aware of the presence of the Croatian army officers. The Judges will evaluate in respect of the documents you have presented and about which the witness has made his comments. I don't think we can go any further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President. I'm just going to move on, at this point, to the next document, which is Exhibit 406/56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Judges will evaluate things, as they always do. I think you also have to get used to a procedure where the Judges can appreciate or evaluate the relevance or irrelevance or the evasiveness of the witness, which I'm saying for the witness, not just this witness in this courtroom. You show your evidence, the witness answers as he wishes to answer, and the Judges make their evaluation. INTERPRETER: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I ask you to take a look at this document that's in evidence, which is a letter from the president of the Travnik HVO, Zeljko Pervan, to President Tudjman, President Franjo Tudjman. If you could look at the second to last page, the paragraph beginning, "It would be very helpful"; do you see that? At the bottom of the page, Brigadier. Let me read it to you, you can probably catch it. The document reads: "It would be very helpful," directing this to President Tudjman of Croatia, "If you could once again instruct your assistants to send senior officers of the Croatian army headed by General Praljak to consolidate our units in the Lasva Valley." The date of this document is the 12th of April 1993, the same date as the order wherein Colonel Blaskic asks for a list of HV officers; do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I couldn't find the proper excerpt. You said page 2?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second to last page, sir, of the letter. The letter is a three-page letter, it's the second page, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it's the bottom paragraph, the bottom paragraph on the second page. I'll read it to you again. "It would be very helpful" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can he please mark it for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Our problem is that we don't have it in Serbo-Croat. We have it on the ELMO, but you have the whole page, except for the line which is the important line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your permission, it would be good that the Croatian text be given to the witness so that he could see the date, signature, the institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, the witness has to have the Croatian text. I don't have to have the French version, but at least give me the English one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's on the last page of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that's not the sentence. We are almost there. Yes, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's up a page, down, the other way, the other way. Down more. The other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It's the other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Usher, it's the other way, the top of the page, not the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There we go. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is a French translation of this in the file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Kehoe. Ask your question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see that line, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Pervan is saying that, once again, he is asking President Tudjman to once again send senior officers from the Croatian army to the Lasva Valley area; isn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would just like to comment on the document itself before I specifically answer your question. This document, as far as I can see, was drafted in the Travnik HVO, which is by the civilian authorities, and Zeljko Pervan, as far as I know, was president of the Travnik HVO, which means it was the civilian authority. This document which I'm holding in my hand I never saw in the Operative Zone command. It can also be seen that it was not delivered to him where you have all the addressees, the three addressees. The sentence which you were referring to would need to be taken in the entirety of the issue relating to the situation in the Travnik municipality; and if we pull it out of the context, and if we just gave answers to these excerpts, we would not get a real picture. So, on the basis of all of this, I can just say and confirm that when the civilian authorities analysed the situation with all the problems that were present in the territory, which was similar to the other municipalities, it came to a conclusion that we did not have enough trained military officers. So, they are setting out this initiative and asking for assistance. However, I know that if this is the time when this document was drafted, at that time there were no officers of the Croatian army in the Operative Zone command, regardless of what the representative of the civilian authorities was requesting. So, this should be taken in the context of the entire situation, in the context of the entire military personnel that was available in the area, and the civilian authorities have concluded there are no officers who could carry out the task for the organisation and system that was established in the territory of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me shift gears here, the document speaks for itself, and we will move away from that document at this point, Brigadier. I would like to change the subject just a bit and talk to you a little bit about the headquarters that was run by then Colonel Blaskic. Tell us a little bit about the headquarters, Brigadier. Can you explain the format, and where people were located, and where the communications centre was, and where the fax machine was, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The organisation of the Operative Zone command, when I arrived there on 1 November 1992, at that time the command was just being accommodated at the Hotel Vitez, and it did not have all the right conditions in terms of the premises we had there. Then the actual structure, the way it was constructed, and everything else that a command headquarters would need to have in war time. Under such circumstances this is how we organised ourselves. The intelligence unit worked in Nova Bila. The packet system was working in the post office building in a basement that was about 100 metres from the hotel, and the rest of us were in the actual hotel building. In one of the larger rooms there, there was the operation centre with a duty desk, and this is where all the personnel from the operations department were, and all the officers, relating to combat activities. Somewhere upstairs there was the logistics department, there was a hallway there which separated the room where the operations centre was, and the room where General Blaskic worked and stayed and where he slept. He didn't have an apartment or house in Vitez; and so, when he would be there, this is where he would spend the night, and this is where he worked during the day, and this is where he would hold briefings, and that's where he would meet the UNPROFOR representatives and any other visitors who arrived who would come to this hotel. So, we worked in improvised circumstances with respect to accommodation and quality of work conditions. So, those were our conditions of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Brigadier, was there a map room in there, in the headquarters, where lines of confrontation were written and where troops were deployed, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and this map was in the Operative Zone, in the operations room of the Operative Zone. This was actually part of my duty, too, to work on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, that was my next question: Who was responsible to keep that up to date? I mean, you noted that you were; who else in the headquarters was responsible to keep that map up to date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All officers were in charge of that. There was another officer who was with me in the operations and training department, and then all the department heads had their own obligations in that regard, so that when the commander came to the room, he would have the most accurate and up-to-date picture. We entered any changes. As we received information from the subordinate units, we would enter them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was this other person that was responsible, who was in operations, that was responsible to keep this map up to date with you? What's his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Mr. Ivica Cosic who worked with me, and for a while it was Mario Rajic, and then he transferred to the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With regard to the actual operation within the headquarters, tell me about a general day. Was there something akin to an orders group meeting every morning that was held by the colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic, or General Blaskic today, had a method of work that every day, whenever he could, he held morning briefings, and very precisely would give out assignments and would debrief every single officer present as to what tasks had to be carried out. If Mr. Blaskic was not around, his Chief of Staff, Mr. Nakic, would hold the briefings. In his absence, it would be myself who held them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is, of course, a traditional or a normal functioning aspect of a headquarters, to have a morning briefing with the commander, or if the commander isn't there, the second in command, or you as chief of operations; that's a normal procedure, is it not, in most headquarters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I would like us to speed things up a bit. I don't know if anyone is challenging the fact that Mr. Blaskic was the chief of the Operational Zone, that he was acting as any Chief of Staff. Let's try to go a bit faster. We're not going to spend weeks and weeks over the question about what Mr. Blaskic did getting up in the morning, going to the office, having his coffee and doing this and that. This is Defence time that is running here. Otherwise, go right to your question. If all of these questions are aimed at trying to get to authenticating something by the witness, please understand that the Judges are intelligent enough to understand what you're doing. I cannot agree to our spending such a long time to know whether he had coffee before going into the map room in Stari Vitez and Vitez. That's what I have to say. Go right to your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These morning briefings, information concerning the situation on the ground was passed back and forth; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was passed back and forth, and this information was based on the reports which we received. So, every morning those units were able to deliver reports, and these reports would end up on the commander's desk, and all that eventually ended up with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During these reporting meetings did the aspects that took place at the Busovaca joint commission, were they discussed during these morning meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regarding the work of the commission, we saw, and I'm talking about the facts regarding the war in the Lasva Valley, on the basis of the joint order of the commander of the Third Corps and the Operative Zone command, on the basis of that, as far as I know, the commander was regularly briefed by the head of this commission, which at that time was Mr. Nakic as Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if Mr. Nakic was told about Muslims being forced to dig trenches by the Busovaca commission, was that subject discussed in these morning briefings by Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Franjo Nakic, when he was a member of the commission in Busovaca, did not come to the morning briefings, because he was tied up in Busovaca. As far as I know, he would come whenever he could, be it in the afternoon or the morning, and personally reported to the commander on the commission's work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was the subject, after the Busovaca joint commission was set up in early February of 1993, and prior to the conflict in April of 1993, was the subject of Muslims being forced to dig trenches discussed at these morning meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall any such discussions, and I'm not aware of that fact, that anyone was forced to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the staff meetings with the people in the headquarters, did Blaskic have regular meetings with his brigade commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Meetings with brigade commanders, in practice, depending on the situation on the ground, were most frequently held once a month, and, I believe, because that is what every commander does, that Commander General Blaskic, during his daily work, as far as communications allowed, he did communicate with the brigade commanders regularly. If the situation were to deteriorate, then the commander would decide when those meetings would be held, and they were held on the basis of a decision and an order of the commander of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend those meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most frequently, yes. Unless I had any other assignment given to me by the commander, because we must realise that this was war and that some officers had other tasks to carry out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any of the meetings that you attended, when Blaskic met with his brigade commanders, did the subject of Muslims being forced to dig trenches, was that subject ever discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty whether this ever happened. I personally do not recall, but I know that Commander Blaskic, though I don't know on the basis of which information, that he did give an order prohibiting any such action. I think that we reviewed such an order when presenting the evidence as to what the Operative Zone commander was doing during the war of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the issuance of that order, and that order was issued on the 19th of June, 1993, after a joint commission meeting, prior to the issuance of that order, had you been in any discussions with headquarters staff or brigade staff where the subject of Muslims being forced to dig trenches came up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not attend. All I know about that is that the Commander of the Operative Zone issued an order expressly prohibiting such action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your conversations during your direct examination, you noted various aspects that were essential for a Commander. Excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, do you want me to go to 11.30 or would you break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we started rather late. Do you have many questions about these trenches dug by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Actually, I am finished that subject at this point. I have a few more questions about the command structures here, we can finish that and take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. You have several questions on the command structures, let's continue with those questions for another few minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, you noted during your direct examination concerning the command structure that what was essential -- and I am reading, counsel, for your purposes, page 12.209 -- what was essential for the operation was five components, actually, six components, planning, organisation, command, coordination, supervision and control. Then a couple of pages later, you noted that, if you had set up an organisation and you had issued commands and orders, the next part of the activity is to ensure that everything was carried out. So you needed to monitor and supervise and these are key factors in a command organisation. Again for clarity in the record, that's page 12.212 of the English transcript. Do you recall that, Brigadier, where you noted that the monitoring of a structure is essential?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, that control of the execution of orders issued is very important. It is also very important that the conditions are in place to enable that supervision to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that monitoring include going out in the field and inspecting the troops and the positions of those troops to ensure that the orders that are being given are being carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Supervision can be done as you have suggested, but it can also be carried out by requesting reports and a feedback report. So there are various possibilities, depending on the one chosen by the Commander, depending on the time available, the kind of activity he wishes to monitor and how important that activity is for the current situation, the war conditions under which we were working and operating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, in direct examination, you noted that the reporting that was coming from the Brigades was not very accurate because of the lack of skilled personnel. Did that cause Colonel Blaskic to monitor activities in the field? By that, did he leave the headquarters frequently to monitor what was happening in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is true that I said that reports due to lack of skill on the part of the officers were incomplete and also because of the concealment of information because they didn't wish some information to reach the Operative Zone Commander. The Commander, General Blaskic, did go to the Brigade commands. I cannot say exactly what he did there, but we as officers too, would occasionally, upon orders of the Commander, go to the Brigade command with the documents we had issued to check whether some thing had been carried out or not. That is whether what had been ordered had been done and how.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did Colonel Blaskic and other members of the Operative Zone staff discover that the Brigades were concealing information from the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be so bold as to say that this was a constant phenomenon. There would be a case of us losing a position on the front-line. The Commander did not wish to report that to the Commander because he hoped he would regain that position and he didn't want to create a negative impression of his ability with the Commander. So he wanted to deal with as many problems as he could by himself within his own zone of responsibility. So that I remember when certain positions fell around the village of Brdo, that we didn't get a report from that Brigade until six or seven hours later. I can't exactly remember how we learned about it and only when we called up did we learn about it and did we have to engage additional forces and try to regain those positions, though they never were regained, they remained the same until the Washington Accords. So that even in such serious instances, that was how the commanders behaved. But that was our reality. I could explain the reasons, an untrained officer, a person who is not qualified for the position he is holding, he is virtually not aware of his responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, what you're saying, Brigadier, is that the lack of accurate information coming to the headquarters was constant and began in 1992 and went through 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and as far as we were able in the command of the Operative Zone, we did everything we could to prevent this, to reduce such tendencies. We would send officers to the commands as assistants in those commands, to set those commands up and to improve them in military terms and improve their organisation to correspond to the aims which we had set ourselves at the end of '92 and the beginning of '93 when we defined our goal of establishing brigades. But this is a painstaking endeavour and I told you what the outcome was at the end of the war. When the MPRI arrived, they noted that a key problem was the control and command, accommodation and funding. Even today, I have a very high position, and those officers, they are retired officers of the American army, they are training us and army officers, as to the way an officer should behave, a NATO officer, a professional officer, what he needs to know, what prior qualities he needs to have and so on. This is for six years. Now we still have similar problems, I can't say they're identical, because we now have peace, but they're similar to what we had in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, did this lack of information, cause Blaskic to go to the front-lines and to send his headquarters officers to the front-lines to monitor and inspect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he do that frequently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "frequently." Do you mean on a daily basis? Every other day? Every five days? Because it is a very imprecise term, frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it part of his routine in organising the command and the control of the Operative Zone to routinely visit front-lines throughout his area of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Blaskic, as far as I know, would go to the commands whenever he, himself, thought it was necessary. I cannot tell you exactly when he felt it was necessary. He was the Commander. We went to carry out supervision when we were ordered to do so by the Commander of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Kehoe, I think we shall have a break now for about twenty minutes, just after quarter to twelve, we will resume work. So the hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed, please have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, just before the break, I asked you a question and I can just read it to you. When I said there was a part of Colonel Blaskic's routine to organise the command and control of the Operative Zone to routinely visit front-lines throughout his area of command and you answered that as far as I know, he would go to the commands whenever he thought it was necessary. My question is dealing with front-line positions and I ask that question again: Did Colonel Blaskic routinely go to front-line positions? As distinguished from Brigade command headquarters, did he routinely go to front-line positions as part of his goal to monitor what was happening in his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Blaskic went to monitor and control whenever he thought it was necessary. So I can't say that he did so routinely, just when it occurred to him. But as a commander and monitoring developments, he would decide when he would go to the Brigade commands and when to the front-lines. As the intervention of General Blaskic was to develop an organisation, as far as I can remember, he wouldn't go to the front-line within the zone of responsibility of a particular Brigade without going to the Brigade command first and going with them to the front-line in order to point to any shortcomings or deficiencies that he may notice. If General Blaskic were to go to the front without the knowledge of the Brigade commander, that would undermine the unity of command and he would thereby be belittling the Brigade commander, who, anyway, didn't enjoy a great deal of authority among their soldiers, among their troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Just a couple of subjects I would like to clear up before we move to an entirely different subject. I would just like to show you an exhibit that has been received in evidence, Prosecutor's Exhibit 292, and there was a Defence exhibit that was the exact same thing, I am just unfamiliar with the number. So if we could just talk about Prosecutor's Exhibit 292. Now I realise this document is in English, Brigadier, however, this is the way it was sent to ECMM and I want to direct your attention, if I could, to the top line. Now, is that the fax number for the Central Bosnian Operative Zone at the top of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly whether that is the number. After all, it was five years ago, so I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, does it say, that is the HVO Central Bosnian Operative Zone with the number after that of 3872711300?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says on this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where was the fax machine in the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fax machine in the headquarters was in the communication centre. As far as I remember, in the course of 1993, we had one installed with the officer on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Colonel Blaskic have his own fax machine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he share this fax machine with others; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not shared it. Everything that was done in the headquarters depended on the Commander. So we all worked to carry out his decisions in the field. Everything depended on the Commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean, for instance, during the course of a day, would using this fax machine, for instance, would the Commander Colonel Blaskic make a determination what press releases were going to leave the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there was a press service which was there to inform the public about events in the area of Central Bosnia. The way in which the officers in the press service communicated with the Commander, I cannot say. I don't know exactly how they reached agreement, but the press service in our organisation was not really part of the actual organisational structure because their responsibilities were different from those of the officers and Chiefs of Staff in the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn to another subject and I just want to clarify something for myself. I can show you Defence Exhibit 200. Now, if you just take a look at the BSC section, you said in your examination that this was a signature of Mijo Bozic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is Mijo Bozic's signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you described Mijo Bozic as a professional soldier and he knows how the structure and control and command functions and that the superior has to be informed about what is happening. For the record that is on page 12.226 of the transcript. Now, my question, Brigadier, is with regard to executing an order such as this. This would be done with the approval of Colonel Blaskic and he would be informed by Mijo Bozic that he had, in fact, signed such an order; is that the procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The procedure was as follows: I said that at the morning briefings we would be given assignments as to what each of the members of the command had to do. We would undertake to carry out those assignments. If the assignment was to issue an order of these contents, as we see here, then General Blaskic would provide the guidelines, the frameworks, as to what should be written and for what purpose. That would be 85 to 90 per cent would be his contribution to the order. It was our duty as officers to draft this, to type it, and to submit it to him for signature. In all occasions, if Blaskic was away, so as not to waste any time, he would give these precise assignments in the morning and say, "Sign on my behalf." When we returned to the headquarters, those orders had to be there waiting for him on his table so that he could see what had been signed in his absence. That was the practice in our headquarters and even today, as the Chief of Staff of the 1st Guards Corps in the army of the federation, I signed the document in the absence of the Commander, but when he comes back, I show him what has actually been written. That is how this document was created too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, suffice it to say that Colonel Blaskic trusted Mijo Bozic to sign this document on his behalf; did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my impression was that General Blaskic trusted his associates; and had Mijo Bozic written something with which General Blaskic did not agree, when he returned and saw the document, Mijo Bozic would have been criticised or whatever, depending on the seriousness of his mistake. The commander would decide what to do. I don't know what he would decide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mijo Bozic was given, shortly after this order in October of 1992, Mijo Bozic was given command over the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak; was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not after this order. When I reached the Operative Zone command he was already there, and I said that I joined on the 1st of November. As far as I remember, Mijo Bozic was appointed to commander in 1993. Please don't hold me to the day of the date, but I think it was in February 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a close relationship between Mijo Bozic and Blaskic that caused them to trust him and give him this honour as a brigade commander? Or did he just have faith in Mijo Bozic as a commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will say what I know with regard to Mijo Bozic and General Blaskic, as persons in their relationship. As far as I know, they did not know each other before the war, though I'm not quite sure; because Mijo Bozic, before the war, was serving in the district staff of Territorial Defence in Zenica. As far as I know, General Blaskic was serving in Slovenia. Whether they may have come across one another as officers of the former army, I don't know. As far as I know, Mijo Bozic was born in Kresevo and General Blaskic was born in Brestovsko, Kiseljak municipality; so again, I cannot connect them. Further, Mijo Bozic is quite a bit older than General Blaskic, in age. I think he was born in 1950 and General Blaskic in 1960, or '61. So, generation-wise they couldn't have gone to school together. However, Mijo Bozic, whom I found in the command when I joined, he was in the operations department, he was head of that department. When he left I took his place; and if a person holds such a position, that is as head of operations department, the commander has to trust you, because if he doesn't, then he would probably look for somebody else whom he trusted more to assign to that position. From the facts that I have presented, I think that General Blaskic did trust Mijo Bozic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just a couple of other questions, Brigadier, just on the flow of paper that I just want to clarify. If we could show these in unison, and we don't have to spend much time on this, Brigadier, Defence Exhibit 338, Defence Exhibit 402, and Defence Exhibit 406, and I just want to focus on the BCS version. 338, 402 and 406. Actually, we can look at all of them in unison, we can look at all of them together, because I just want to ask you some questions about some writing on them. Do you have those three documents before you, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I have the three documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you clarify something for me? Is the writing in those three documents in the right-hand corner, is that all your writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the right-hand corner the words "Urgent for Kiseljak and Busovaca," that is my handwriting and my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose writing is next to yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Next to mine, as far as I recall, this could be the handwriting of Franjo Sliskovic, who was assistant for logistics. Because you see I have written "urgent for Kiseljak," I'm sending it to Kiseljak where the commander was; but I'm also sending it to Busovaca where Franjo Sliskovic lived, so that the matter should be dealt with as quickly as possible, because I was cognisant of the seriousness of the request by Rasim Delic, because I received the document from the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could it be clear that this is D402, the record didn't reflect which document he was looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I was waiting for the Brigadier to finish and follow-up. That is D402, counsel is a hundred per cent correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other two documents, 338 and 406, the initials ONO; are those initials yours, as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which document are we referring to, 406?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Either 406 -- 406, just for clarification's sake, is dated the 22nd of April. It's not the 22nd of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's the 26th of January, 1992, I believe, D406.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, counsel, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: D406 is the 26th of January, 1992; is that your initials there, too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The word "done" or "executed" and the initials are mine, and ONO is mine, because I did everything that I was supposed to do, which was my competence. Yes, all that is in my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that kind of a routine thing to do when it comes to your attention, to put your initials on it in some capacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no regulations, so, you couldn't say that it was a routine thing, because there are also some documents where I did not put this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 338, the next document, does that ONO belong to you? I think that's the document, unless I'm incorrect here, the 22nd of April; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, here it is stated in this document, the letters ONO were hand-written by me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you a document, Brigadier, and I'll ask if you can recognise this handwriting, if I can, with the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document 478.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at that writing, Brigadier; do you recognise that writing? Is that yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recognise this handwriting, and it is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the writing on the bottom, is that handwriting yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this is not my handwriting, either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't recognise who wrote this? You don't recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not recognise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Let's move to another subject. The subject we're going to move to is the actual army itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: May I have the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 478.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, apologies, this document is only in Croatian version, and nobody in this room, with the exception of Mr. Marin and myself and maybe another person or two, would know what this means; because as it stands now it looks like a mysterious document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I invite the Brigadier to read it into the record. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, even though it is not your handwriting, could you read it into the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I thought you were right, Mr. Nobilo; but I thought that the Prosecutor's question was simply to know whether this was the person who wrote the document. In fact, this might be of interest to know what the contents are. Perhaps you might read it to us and then the interpreters will interpret it for us, unless you do not want to ask that question, Mr. Kehoe, the decision is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I don't want any mystery about what this document says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Since it's only three-and-a-half lines, we can read it. Read it, please, and the interpreters will interpret it. Please read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, this document states as follows: "All military conscripts shall report to their military command," and the rest of the word is missing, and then "the HVO units." At the bottom it says, "For the press, the Travnik HVO and Novi Travnik".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let's move to another subject, and I would like to address testimony you talked about during your direct, and you were answering some questions by Mr. Nobilo and counsel, I'm talking about page 12.051, and you were talking about some of the problems that you had in the HVO as a whole. I could just read a portion of your testimony. You said, "First of all, the entire organisation was based on voluntariness, which made difficult, the functioning of the chain of command." Down on line 13, "Voluntariness, in simple terms, implies that a soldier or conscript applies on a voluntary basis to join. Similarly, he is free to leave a certain organisation because you have no instrument when he is a volunteer to fit him within the structure, because of the overall situation in which you are working and living." You again reiterated that problem, sir, on page 12.092, when you talked about one of the major problems being the voluntary principle. Now, sir, let me direct your attention to Prosecutor's Exhibit 36/1, if I could.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We would need a few minutes to find it in the vault of the Registry since we don't have it with us here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We can continue and I will read it into the record, and we can go back on it, if need be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, what I'm reading to you is Article 3 from the Narodni List, published on the 3rd of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Which came from where? Narodni List, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's called the National Gazette, they call it the Narodni Lists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 3: "Every citizen of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna shall have the duty to protect and defend the independence and territorial integrity of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna; and therefore, the obligation to: One, serve in the army; two, perform compulsory work service; three, participate in Civil Defence; four, participate in monitoring and reporting services; five, be subject to requisition." Are you familiar with that aspect of the law, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that there was a regulation. I think that it was called something, a decree on the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna. However, this document was compiled as a foundation for the organisation and structure of the army which we wanted to establish and build. In accordance, on the basis of this document, you saw that a number of other documents were drafted both by Mr. Blaskic and others in order to accomplish this goal. But the situation on the ground was indeed as I presented it, and I think that you will find the documents drafted by Colonel Blaskic, which I believe have already been tendered here, where he refers to the voluntariness should be abolished, that these decrees should be implemented and so on and so forth. However, in order to implement such a law, this law is a foundation, but you needed instruments, instrument of a state. We did not have this state. So this was a process of establishing an army in wartime conditions. You had a war against the army of Republika Srpska, in comparison to which we were poorly armed, and then, despite this law, people would show up and wanted to join. They showed up at the local headquarters. So, this initial principle of voluntariness was gradually diminishing. People realised that it is not just a simple thing to go to war, because people were dying in the war. Another aspect which contributed to this situation is that we also mentioned that there were instances of crime that, for instance, we had a situation that somebody went to the front-line at Jajce, and criminals would then operate and they would simply take some property or things like that. So, what you're referring to, this was a framework for establishment of a military which we wanted to have, which we desired to have; but I said that, I mentioned the reasons why we did not have this. I also mentioned that one of the principles of the organisation of the HVO was this voluntariness, and we had this situation that, let's say a soldier spent ten days at the front-line, and because of the needs, three days later he would need to go again. But he refused, he says let's send someone else. So this is a real situation which is hard to comprehend unless a person was really there in the theatre, to see how things were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on this article, and based on this law, on the 3rd of July, 1992, compulsory military service was introduced into Herceg-Bosna; was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If this is what is written in this document, then that is the case, but I do not have the document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we have it now in this BCS Article 3.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document here that is 36A of the Prosecutor, if that's the one you want to show.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. We can move ahead, Mr. President, and come back to that particular point on that. INTERPRETER: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Here it is, okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, based on that article, my question is: Was compulsory military service introduced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of this article, yes, the conscription is mandatory. As I wanted to point out, we could not have established the HVO on no basis, but everything that is mentioned here, all the provisions, were envisaged as a basic document for the establishment of an organisation that would be as good as possible under the circumstances in a given time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Blaskic implemented conscription right away; didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apologies, when we talk about conscription, we have to be very specific, because conscription has two meanings. So, could you please specify which aspect of conscription you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did he, based on this principle, immediately implement the compulsory military service component and abolish the voluntary principle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Blaskic or Colonel Blaskic was not authorised for this work. This was a kind of competence of the territorial staff of the defence department at municipal levels. I was working in such an office at one time, so I am familiar with this. If these instruments existed, then such a person can conscript of a particular individual and if this individual does not respond to it, he could be prosecuted. If on the second notice, this individual does not appear, then the case may be sent from the defence office down to the civilian police and they would then issue a warrant for arrest. But when a person is finally in the uniform, then he is under the authority of a Commander and as soon as he takes off his uniform, he is a civilian again. I know this very well because I worked in such an office of defence for five years. I was running such an office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take a look at Defence Exhibit 199, which is dated the 10th of May, 1992, some two months prior, or almost two months prior, to the actual decree coming down. This is the 10th of May, 1992, order, introduced by the Defence, signed by the Colonel, Blaskic. Now, Brigadier, you, when you were being questioned on direct examination, you focused namely on No. 1, but I would like you to read No. 7. Now, I remind you that this is the 10th of May, 1992, and the actual decree in acting come compulsory military service was the 3rd of July; nevertheless, on the 10th of May, 1992, at Point 7, Blaskic says as follows: "I forbid all persons, subject to military conscription, in the Kiseljak municipality, as well as other civilians who may be needed by the armed forces of the HVO or armed formations of the HVO, to leave the borders of the municipality without permission of the HVO. Commanders of the military police units are personally responsible for the execution of this task." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn to another document. If I may, this is not a document that has been received in evidence yet. This is a document where, apparently, the translation section or I couldn't actually read the actual date because it has a stamp on there, but it is in May 1992, signed by Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 479, 479A for the French version; B for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, on the order itself -- I'm sorry, just move the next one to the ELMO. That's it. Do you recognise that stamp or that signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this is a stamp from Kiseljak, which I am not familiar with and a signature I am not familiar with either. Somebody signed this on behalf of the person whose name is typed there. I don't recognise the signature though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the person's name who is typed there is Tihomir Blaskic, is it not? Or Tiho Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not clearly legible, but from the four letters that I can make out, you could infer that it is Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's read it, sir. "Due to the fact that the barracks in Kiseljak need to be put in order, in a quicker and more efficient way and taking into consideration the possibility of engaging persons eligible for military service who have not yet been called up, I am issuing the following order: 1. A certain number of persons eligible for military service is to be engaged in labour units. 2. Labour units will carry out their activities in a planned and organised manner from 09.00 to 17.00 according to the plan of engagement. 3. Women can be engaged in labour units on a voluntary basis." Then it talks about units, the composition and the transportation and who was going to organise it. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we noted before in the article that's before you, that the actual order for compulsory military service was issued on the 3rd of July, 1992. I ask you to take a look at Exhibit 456/94. Now, Brigadier, this is a document of Colonel Blaskic. It says, "Regional staff Central Bosnia with Gornij Vakuf, Strictly confidential, No. 93/92, 4 July 1992. On the basis of the announcements and reports of the Operative Zone commanders of 3 July, 1992, and in order to improve the combat readiness of the Central Bosnia HVO units, I hereby issue the following order: And go down to number 3, sir. "According to the needs of the HVO armed forces, municipal staff, the principle of compulsory service is introduced and the voluntary principle is abolished." That should be number 2, I apologise. "According to the needs of the armed force municipal staff, the principle of compulsory military service is introduced and the voluntary principle is abolished for all those aged between 18 and 55 who are liable for military service." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, sir, staying with that order, if you could turn to No. 6. No. 6 states that it's an order to intensify propaganda activities in order to boost morale and create a sense of insecurity in the enemy.
