Is that a normal thing for a commander to do, order that propaganda activities should be boosted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a situation when you are facing a much more powerful enemy and in considering the time when this document was drafted and this was the army of Republika Srpska and it is well established what their strength was in comparison to both the BH army and the HVO. When you have the battles at Kupres, Livno and Ravno, then you could do anything to lift the morale and this task makes sense in that context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Blaskic put himself in charge of the propaganda activities, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Within the Operative Zone command there was information, a propaganda department. That means that people who were tasked with informing the soldiers through their representatives of the events, what was going on, what steps were taken, whether it was going to be harder the next day or easier. In military terms, this was done precisely in the way that General Blaskic did here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, nevertheless, going back to Point 2 in this order, clearly Blaskic orders compulsory military service and abolishes the voluntary principle. Now, let me show you yet another order of Colonel Blaskic. This is dated the 19th of September, 1992. Mr. Usher?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Document 480; 480A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now this is an order, is it not, Brigadier, the 19th of September, 1992, by Colonel Blaskic, coming from the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, does he sign that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is General Blaskic's signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In No. 6, we'll read the preparatory paragraph and then move to No. 6. You're welcome to read the entire document, naturally. But on the basis of reports, a proposal by members of the headquarters, a personal review of the situation on the field and following an evaluation with the purpose of rectifying mistakes I order: This goes to the municipal headquarters Commander. "Submit a list of people eligible for the military who left the municipality on their own initiative." Do you see that, sir? Do you see that Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To implementing the compulsory service in July, you would agree with me that Blaskic is trying to go after potential conscripts who have left the area; isn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot agree with you that General Blaskic could introduce the obligatory military service. This is something prescribed by the state. The documents that we have reviewed just now and which were issued before the decree on the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna and the decree on the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna came into being as a document that were not based on anything before that. Because, before the establishment of Herceg-Bosna, there was a military service obligation. The obligation to provide material resources and all the other obligations. So, actually, the law that was in effect until then was taken over. On those grounds, all the documents were drafted, which the Commander of the Operative Zone or the Commander in Kiseljak issued before the publication of the decree on the armed forces of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. But in the preamble of each of these documents, reference is made to what preceded it. Because we must realise that we couldn't wait for the decree on the armed forces to stop the army of Republika Srpska at Livno, Kupres, Jajce and Ravno and so on. Before any such document was issued, the army of Republika Srpska attacked Ravno, Sarajevo and all those other places, so no commander could wait. He had to do what he could in view of the difficult circumstances. So that commanders with experience and being aware of the legal regulations in force in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina issued such orders. Because the defence departments that existed in the municipalities were functioning and operating on the basis of the legal regulations of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina until the regulations of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna were passed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What date is this order that is before you, Brigadier? What date is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 19th of September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's over two months after the decree was passed ordering compulsory service, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I tried to be precise in my answer. All the orders that were issued before the decree was passed, the decree of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna emanated from the existing regulations of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So, if a decree was issued before this document that I have before me, then this document was based on that decree. I am ready to answer any specific question regarding this order in front of me. But could those questions be clear? Because I am very familiar with these matters and I may be of use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Brigadier, but the question was a very precise one. This decree, this document, came two months after the decree. So I am here to regulate the overall hearings. The question was very precise. You can't always say that the question was not precise. The question was very precise. This order is dated 19th of September, '92, two months after the decree. The question was very precise. You can just say that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next document, Brigadier, Exhibit 456/81 dated 7th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could ask for 456/3, I think we can move through these documents more quickly, Mr. President. We're looking at, the first one is 456/81 and the next one is 456/3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, the document that's in your hands, again another document that is sent by packet by Colonel Blaskic is dated the 7th of October, 1992, three months after the compulsory service was enacted. I turn your attention -- and again you're welcome to read the entire document -- I turn your attention to Point 3 where Blaskic orders: "Commanders of the municipal headquarters of Kakanj and Kresevo must bring along as well, a copy of the order, call up order, regarding conscripts and their departure to the front-line." He references the Narodni List, No. 1, page 60, regarding failure and refusal to carry out orders. Now, he is ordering commanders in Kakanj and Kresevo to bring a list of conscripts, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he is ordering that because we were already having a problem with the response to the call up and going to the front-line. He is referring to the regulation on the basis of which certain measures can be taken by competent defence departments and that the Brigade should show them those regulations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about that. Let's turn to the next document, which is 456/3, which is dated 11 November, 1992. Again, a packet communication, and I direct your attention to 21 and 23. Now, is this a packet communication, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It doesn't say packet communications, but judging by the appearance of the document, it probably arrived through packet communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just read this, sir. Beginning with the preparatory language and then we'll move directly to paragraph 21 and 23 respectively: "In view of the current military situation in Central Bosnia Operative Zone, which was considered in detail at a meeting held 6th November of 1992. A subsequent discussion of the gentleman present with the aim of strengthening defence and consolidating forces, I hereby order: 21. The conscripts who refuse to be sent to the front are to be disarmed and brought to the appropriate command under the jurisdiction of the regional military police. 23. A list of conscripts who work abroad is to be made in the HVO government decision on donations where defence is to be implemented." Now, Blaskic, in the order that we saw on the 4th of July, implements the compulsory conscription. He asks his commanders for lists of conscripts. In this order, he wants a list of conscripts who are outside the country, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He is asking his commanders and those commanders will address themselves to the defence departments because those departments were aware of the movement of military conscripts because they kept records of all military conscripts within the territory of a municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this mobilisation continued throughout 1992 and throughout 1993 and throughout the entire time Blaskic was in as the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We never managed fully to engage all potential military conscripts who were listed in the records of the municipalities, and we didn't for reasons visible from these documents. Some people were abroad before the war, never came back. Some people afraid of the war fled. We have such people in the west living as refugees. General Blaskic, whose duty was to set up an organisation and to have insight into the potential effectives he had at his disposal, so he searched for information of this kind in this way. However, from the first part of this document, it can be seen that a decision to issue it was made at a meeting, but we can't see whether representatives of the civilian authorities, the political authorities, were present. But I assume that all the tasks assigned in this order were agreed upon at that meeting, so that all the responsible institutions who were operational at the time would recognise their responsibilities. Then this order went to the commanders so that they would know what decisions had been taken at the meeting and also to be able to refer to this document when contacting the defence departments with which they cooperated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, the bottom line is that service in the HVO was compulsory; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was stated in the decree. I said that and I am not denying it, nor can it be denied. This was stated in the decree. But the situation underground was such as you can see within two or three months you had to issue five orders in order to try to implement that. We didn't manage to implement it even when the Washington Accords were signed because the situation as it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's about two minutes to one and I am about to shift into another subject area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, we'll resume with that new subject at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.59 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed, please have the accused brought in, and the witness. (The accused entered court) (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours, very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, just a couple more questions on this voluntariness issue that you discussed during your direct examination with Mr. Nobilo. You noted that that voluntariness issue also permeated the military police, because there were no standards for the military police; do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regarding the military police, I said that they joined voluntarily, which meant that young men who wanted to join the military police would report to military police commanders in their place of residence, and they would join the military police. There was no special selection or any standards that would impose certain requirements that you had to fulfil to become a member of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you said was that the member of the military police came on a voluntary basis and there were no criteria established for someone to become a member of the military police. I'm reading page 12.080, and I ask you to take a look at the next exhibit, sir. With the assistance of the usher, it's right here. One of those rare occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 481, 481A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, I apologise there is no French, Mr. President, but that's in translation, as well, or will be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, do you know Zvonko Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know Zvonko Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Zvonko Vukovic, as it relates to the military police, for the 4th Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zvonko Vukovic was a military police commander. I cannot tell you exactly from when until when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Zvonko Vukovic was ultimately replaced by Pasko Ljubicic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn the page -- well, actually, you're looking at it, you see the stamp in the lower right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the incoming stamp. As far as I can remember, this is not the incoming stamp of the Operative Zone command; but as the police had its own communications system, this was probably the incoming stamp of the police, or the HVO in Travnik. So, I'm not quite sure whose incoming stamp this is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is also another communication that appears to be sent by the packet communication system; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's read this document, Brigadier. It's dated 11th of January, 1993, and it's addressed to HVO military police stations in the municipalities of Travnik, Novi Travnik, Vitez, Zenica, Busovaca, Kresevo, Kiseljak, Fojnica, Vares, and Kakanj. It reads as follows: "As part of the reorganisation project of the military police in the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, we are about to form special purpose units of the military police. In order for all the regions of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna to be equally represented in these units, you are hereby requested to propose five of your members for this purpose, before 15 January, 1993. The members are to become full-time employees of the military police and will carry out their duties throughout the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. Temporary headquarters of these will be in Capljina. Requirements for admission: Secondary school education; maximum age 30; membership in the HVO prior to the announcement of general mobilisation for June 1992; completion of the military police or regular police training; prior service as a military policeman in the former JNA or a member of its special units. The following data should be submitted for each candidate who meets the above requirements: Name, father's name, and surname, date of birth, place and municipality of birth, residence address, education and speciality, rank and military record in the JNA, information on all training completed so far, date of joining the Croatian army, HV or the HVO, name of all the units in which the candidate has served since joining the HV or the HVO, commanders opinion on performance up until now. Please observe the deadline." Now, sir, this is the setting up of the unit known within the military police, known as the Jokeri, or the Jokers; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could not confirm that on the basis of this document, because that is not stated in this document, that it has to do with the Jokers; but it does refer to the organisation of a professional military police, as is stated here. When I was making my testimony and said that people joined the military police on a voluntary basis, this applied to the police at the level of the municipality. But you see here that the commander is addressing the police at the level of municipal police bodies, asking for candidates; so, we're talking about professional military policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Brigadier, that for the special purpose units formed within the military police in January of 1993, significant criteria were required for the candidates to be admitted into this special purpose unit? Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know which unit was formed on the 11th of January, 1993, because the internal organisation of the military police is something I'm not very familiar with; but all I can say is what I can see from this text, and it says that it is full-time employment, which means military policemen will be professionals, and that they will be operating throughout the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. There is no specific mention of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you about the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Brigadier. There was a special purpose unit within the 4th Military Police Battalion in Central Bosnia; wasn't there? Specifically in the Central Bosnian Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, and I said that I couldn't discuss the internal structure and organisation of the military police because I was not familiar with it. It was not a problem addressed by the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. I think that it had about 15 policemen. How it was formed, what it was transformed into later on, I cannot tell you exactly, because, I wish to repeat, the internal structure of the military police was not within the terms of reference of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. As an officer in that Operative Zone, I did not supervise the military police, because we had no such authority in relation to the military police. But this document says that, refers to the formation of a professional military police for the whole area of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, was the Jokeri a special purpose unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, that is how they were called. As far as I can remember, there were about 15 military policemen in that unit, but I'm not sure about these figures, as I have said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Jokeri was stationed at the Bungalow on the road right outside of Ahmici; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that there was a unit, or a part of the 4th Battalion in the Bungalow, exactly which unit, I cannot tell, but I do know that it was a military police unit. Whether it was the Jokers or something else, I think there was also a general police and traffic police; so, I cannot, with certainty, talk about the structure of the 4th Military Police Battalion because I am not familiar with it. This is a structure that was not determined by the commander of the Operative Zone, but rather the military police administration attached to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, one moment, I just want to consult with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, we would like to move on. INTERPRETER: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can move on to a separate subject, and again, I want to just chat with you for a couple of moments, Brigadier, about your testimony with Mr. Nobilo last week. One of the things that you mentioned was that you noted, and this is on page 12.074, that one of the problems you had with the troops was that there was no real facilities. You said on line 7 on 12.074 that, "it was very difficult because of the lack of proper facilities, to build proper military discipline." Then you went on to say on -- excuse me, before that, on page 12.067, that "the difficulty with combat ready forces means personnel in one place in a barracks which have their duties and are undergoing training and which are adequately equipped." Do you remember those statements you said about the lack of proper facilities, having some difficulty in training your people and keeping control over the troops? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, and today the HVO has certain problems with facilities and accommodation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you a document, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 482, 482A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, this is a decree signed by the president of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna on the 3rd of July, 1992, where the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna took over all the JNA facilities. Let's read this: "Pursuant to Article 7 of the decision on establishing the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna of 18 November, 1991, the presidency of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna at its session --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I do not have that document in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We also have a different document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have the document numbered 482.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think there is a problem here. We have to look at the date in the Serbo-Croatian version, and the date on the third line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's part of the Narodni Lists that are in evidence in Exhibits 36, 37 and 38, and I can read the English and withdraw that exhibit, and I can point to the place in the Narodni List where it exists already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read this to you, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Kehoe. I think what Mr. Nobilo is saying is that the text in BCS and the English text that I have don't seem to match.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If the Narodni List is going to be read from, could the witness please be shown the entire document from which it is going to be read?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will find it at the break, Brigadier. Let me ask you a question just about the JNA facilities.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If you allow me, for the transcript, it would be better to clarify the situation so we know what number we're going to use for which document, because there are two documents that don't match.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, your intention, apparently, was to confront the witness with a decree which was signed by Mate Boban the 3rd of July, 1992; is that what you intended to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If that is your intention, then you have to find the Serbo-Croatian text for this document which has the number 482.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question about the JNA facilities. Did the HVO take over the JNA facilities in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation regarding facilities of the former JNA in the area of Central Bosnia was as follows: The Travnik barracks, which was held by the former JNA, was liberated jointly by the HVO and the BH army units. After the control was taken of this barracks, I cannot say who it was initially, but after the fall of Kotor Varos in Jajce, I know the refugees were accommodated there, and units of both the BH army and the HVO from Kotor Varos. Due to the proximity of the lines with the army of the Republika Srpska and the potential danger of being shelled, we did not use these barracks. After the attack against HVO by the BH army, this barracks came under control of the BH army. The facility of the former JNA in Kaonik, and another one in the Busovaca municipality, were depots and Kaonik, even to date, these facilities are not properly outfitted for accommodating the army. Then the third facility of the former JNA was in Kiseljak municipality. I know that this was not a large facility, and I know that these barracks, during the war, the units, or the special purposes unit of Kiseljak were accommodated there. Further, there was barracks in Zenica which also were liberated, jointly, by the BH army and the HVO units, and then later on it was completely taken over by the BH army. Then there was another depot at Slimena, and it was a facility which was used exclusively as a weapons and equipment depots. All these facilities were liberated jointly by the HVO and the BH army. Some of these facilities were destroyed at the pull out and some of them were mined, and the HVO did not make any use of that. These facilities were all in the zone of responsibility of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and I believe that I have not omitted any of them. In these circumstances we did not have a potential to keep troops there to train them, and due to this lack of such facilities, we were using school buildings and similar facilities, we improvised and we could not accommodate significant forces there. In these conditions a number of these facilities were, therefore, not in use; but the military organisation continued to keep their troops in the villages from where people were recruited to go to the defence lines. This was one of the problems, because people did not like to go to the barracks. Even if we had them, it would have been difficult to keep people in them. Had we had them where we could have brought people and trained them there, we would have done so, but you have to keep one thing in mind: The shelling was always possible, both by the air force and by the artillery, which was in possession of the army of the Republika Srpska, and this was at all times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, who took the Kaonik camp, the JNA facility at Kaonik on the Busovaca T junction? Who took that? HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Kaonik facility, which is at that T junction, was taken over by the Busovaca HVO, and this was another facility which was a depot which did not have a potential for accommodating larger armed force. Because the former JNA had also not used it for training of soldiers who were serving in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took the Draga barracks; the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that the Draga barracks were taken over by the HVO, but the facility is such that it is exclusively a depot. Even to date, it is used by the HVO. But even to date, we cannot accommodate the troops, the parts of the 3rd Guard Corps, because these are specifically warehouse facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a facility that you didn't talk about that's near your hometown of Novi Travnik and that's the JNA facility at Stojkovici, the HVO took that as well, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I forget that. It is a facility -- it is a logistics base and this facility was designated by the former JNA for storage of larger quantities of fuel. So this again is a special use facility where, I think, that not even 100 people can be accommodated, so this is again a depot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HVO used the JNA facility at Stojkovici as a communication centre, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that, so I cannot speak to that. I do not know. Maybe because there are some underground facilities, it was used as a protection from potential shelling or air attacks from the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now Kiseljak, as we move down to the road, Kiseljak, the largest former JNA facility was in the Kiseljak barracks; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the largest in relation to what? For instance, the barracks in Sarajevo are the largest. So, if you can tell me what to compare it to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the Kiseljak barracks, the former JNA facility at the Kiseljak barracks, the HVO took that facility as well; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO took over this facility and I said that as far as I know, as early as wartime, this was used by Maturice or whatever this special purpose unit was called in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it was used by Blaskic too, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this barracks, in one of the buildings there, and I don't know, I didn't go there at that time. It could have been the Brigade command. I did not go to Kiseljak when the commander at Kiseljak was General Blaskic. I was in Novi Travnik at that time and I was not in the Operative Zone command at that time, so I cannot speak to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, you told us during fighting in and around Busovaca in January and February that Blaskic was in Kiseljak and that you were communicating with him in the Kiseljak barracks; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was in Kiseljak at that time in 1993. That was that Kiseljak already had a Brigade and it had its command post there in Kiseljak. But I told you first that I did not know where the municipal headquarters in Kiseljak was and we saw from certain documents that this was when General Blaskic was commander there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The bottom line, Brigadier, is that in addition to the units you were talking about, Colonel Blaskic used the Kiseljak barracks too, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Has this been asked and answered, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Hayman. I'm sorry to have to tell you that we're not getting an answer. I don't accept your intervention, Mr. Hayman. The witness is contradicting himself, you know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please don't continue going down that line of comments. I do understand that Mr. Kehoe is going back to that issue, I understand. We don't know whether the relationship with what was before, we don't know what that was. We know he was in Kiseljak, but not at that time, maybe not that barracks. We can understand that these are questions that the Prosecutor want to know from someone who was in such an important position. Ask your question again, Mr. Kehoe, the Judges need to know. I would ask the witness to make special efforts to jog his memory. Work on this please, General. You're bound to do so by the text of the Tribunal. You cannot remember all kinds of things when you're the defence witness and no, for every question that's asked you, say, you don't know or not aware of it. I really very firmly have to commit you to answering completely the questions that are asked, otherwise the Judges are going to have to ask you the questions. Ask your question again, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, Colonel Blaskic used the Kiseljak barracks during his work, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Can we have a time, Mr. President? That's why there is confusion here. General Blaskic was in Kiseljak in the summer of '92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, the question was not asked of you, the question was asked of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let the witness answer instead of you, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, in 1992, at the time when General Blaskic was Commander of the Kiseljak municipal headquarters, and I do not know the exact time frame, I do not know whether during that period his command post was in the Kiseljak barracks. When we established a Brigade, which was the end of 1992, I know that the command of the Ban Jelacic Brigade was in the Kiseljak barracks. In 1993, that is after the January conflict, between the BH army and the HVO in the territory of the Busovaca and Kiseljak municipality, the then Commander of the Operative Zone, Tihomir Blaskic, was in the Kiseljak barracks at the post of the Operative Zone Commander. Now, which forces were there at that time, I am unable to tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in January, Brigadier, when you were sending fax communications to Colonel Blaskic, where did you send them in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were -- that is when we send them through the packet system and by fax, while General Blaskic was in Kiseljak, we sent it to the command post of the Ban Jelacic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you noted previously that one of the reasons that you didn't do training in the barracks was because you were afraid of Bosnian Serb shelling; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the reason that I refer to only the Travnik barracks, which we were using jointly with the BH army. After the fall of Jajce, after the fall of Kotor Varos, after the BH and the HVO units from Kotor Varos, along with the refugees, arrived, we were unable to use this facility because these people, these people and these soldiers who arrived from those areas were accommodated there from the territory which was taken by the units of the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But during the conflict in January, the Kiseljak barracks was safe enough for the Commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone to work from; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Commander probably did work at that command post. I do not know all his movements over a 24 hour period while he was staying in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move to the next subject, Mr. President, consistent with the Court's request, we do have the Mate Boban order in French and English. We haven't quite collated it, however, here is the BCS version and here is the French version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Document 482 in BSC version, B is the French version and 482A is the English version as was assigned a short while back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at 482, Brigadier --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at 482, Brigadier, that is, in fact, the decree of the 3rd of July, 1992, signed by Mr. Boban on the taking over of the JNA and federal secretariat of peoples defence material on the territory of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna and transforming it into the property of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. "Article 1: All social assets on the territory of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna that has been as federation assets, administered and managed by the former JNA and the former SSNO, shall be taken over and shall become the property of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna and social assets comprise property, money and rights. Article 2: The Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, presidency or an authority authorised by it, shall allocate assets mentioned in Article 1 of the present decree. Article 3: The heads of the defence, legal and administration departments, shall be authorised to issue regulations and comment and documents for the implementation of this decree. Article 4: The decree shall come into the effect on the day that it is issued. Signed Mate Boban, the Presidency of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. Mostar 3 July, 1992." Are you aware of that decree, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not familiar with this decree or this document. I have, personally, not seen before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise either the stamp or the signature of Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have heard of President Boban. I have never met him and I do not know his signature. However, if I may, I would like to say something regarding this document. From the position at which I occupied at the time, this document was drafted, but we had a situation such as I have described it and along with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, this is the way things are now. The situation in the entire territory of the Croatian community was such that it could not have been implemented everywhere. We, in Central Bosnia, were unable to implement it fully. With respect with some facilities of the former JNA, we had to do in a way which I have just described a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you noted during the course of your testimony with Mr. Nobilo that you had a difficult time training your soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did have such difficulties because we don't have teams of instructors, we did not have the compounds where we could train.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, isn't it true, Brigadier, that by mid-1992, into the fall of 1992, a rather elaborate training structure had been set up by the HVO throughout Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know this. That was not the case in Central Bosnia. If I may, all training that was done was conducted with small arms. We had different types of small arms, which was used by the infantry. If a soldier had not handled such a weapon during his regular military service, we would conduct special training and we would, typically, do it a day or two before he would go out to the front-lines so that he would be able to actually use it at the line of defence. We would prevent incidents so that he would not mishandle this weapon. But at the level of platoon company and battalions, this would be the tactical type of training we did not have time for and we did not have conditions for such training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's explore that a little, Brigadier. Let me first show you a film that was filmed, Mr. President, by ITN, in October of 1992, in the Tomislavgrad area. If we could just dim the lights and put this particular film on. It's about five minutes long, Mr. President. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Dim the lights, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Could you dim the lights, please. (Videotape played).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, are you familiar with any HVO training facility such as that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You said at the beginning that what we have just seen was shot in the territory of Tomislavgrad; this was a municipality within the zone of responsibility of the Operative Zone of north-western Herzegovina, and I was not familiar with what was happening in that Operative Zone. But, from what we have seen on this clip, it is visible that it is a reconnaissance sabotage unit, two platoons in strength; because I did serve in Tomislavgrad after the Washington Accords, the people in Tomislavgrad told me they had such a unit which was within the scope of the Tomislavgrad Brigade in Tomislavgrad. This kind of training, and this level of equipment of troops and units is something that we did not have in the command of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. The best equipped and best trained unit in the command of Central Bosnia during the war was a special purpose unit, the Vitezovi. It was structured and organised as such. Its organisation and the equipment of its members was not within the competence of the Operative Zone command. The brigades for which we were responsible and were under our command did not have this kind of training shown on this clip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, the HVO, in addition to training in Central Bosnia, sent people to train elsewhere; didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we sent groups, or perhaps certain servicemen, for training with air defence devices. Because of the special purpose industry in Central Bosnia, the air force of the Bosnian Serbs was constantly shelling this area, so we would send people to train in Herzegovina, people who would man the rocket launchers, Maljutkas, and also some people for reconnaissance training, I think in Grude. That's as much as I know about the organised training undertaken for members of brigades within the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You sent some people to train in Herzegovina and some reconnaissance people to train in Grude. How about people to the Republic of Croatia; did the HVO and Central Bosnia send people to train in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the very beginning of 1992, I don't know, because I said when I joined the command of the Operative Zone. After the enclave was completely cut off, we had no chance of going anywhere after that, and still less to send people to train outside the territory of the Lasva Valley or Bosnia, because we needed every man in the trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, prior to the outbreak of activities in Central Bosnia in January of 1993, did the HVO, to your knowledge, send troops to Croatia to train?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We never sent troops, we sent a group of men, three, four or five men. I cannot confirm exactly what kind of training it was. I think it was military police training, but I'm not quite sure of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times did Blaskic send groups of men to train in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the time I joined the command of the Operative Zone, and that is the 1st of November, 1992, I do not remember that we ever sent people for training to the Republic of Croatia. I do not remember. If there was such a case, by any chance, it may have been an individual or a group of three or four people, up to ten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when did Blaskic send these individuals to some type of police training in the Republic of Croatia? When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot claim that General Blaskic sent these people, because the training of individuals or groups in military police matters was not conducted while General Blaskic was commander of the Operative Zone. If there was any such training, it was through the military police organisation, so that we, as the command of the Operative Zone, could not send military policemen for that kind of training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take a look at Exhibit 406/23.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dubuisson, do we have a number for the film?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, for the video, the number is 483.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this document, 406, again, a packet communication from Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, 24 July, 1992, "On the basis of a clear need to create and train reconnaissance units, I hereby order: Deploy one squad of men for reconnaissance operations in every operation zone, i.e., all municipal headquarters engaged in war operations. Training will take place in the Republic of Croatia, because specific tasks are to be carried out. The training will last ten days. Each of the following municipal headquarters shall appoint seven soldiers to the squad; Gornji Vakuf, Bugojno, Konjic, Jajce, Novi Travnik, Travnik, Zepce, Zavidovici, Maglaj. Deliver the list of men for training through a radio packet communications or by courier by 27 July, 1992 at 1400 hours. The personnel on the list, i.e. the men selected for the training, must report in Grude on 30 July 1992 by 1400 hours. The men must present themselves in the above-mentioned place and time in full combat gear." The document in the original BSC has a list of seven men written down by someone. Now, are you familiar with this procedure of sending at least reconnaissance units for training in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the heading one can see that the document was dated the 24th of May, 1992, when I was not in the Operative Zone, and in my statement before your question I said that as far as I remember I knew that groups did go for training. I know there was mention of Grude, and that groups of men went there from each of the municipal headquarters, but I do not know whether people, other groups, were sent in this way. We can just see from this that training was for ten days, and you can judge for yourself whether ten days is enough to become an expert in reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Correction, the transcript says May 1992, but the witness said in July 1992. So, could the transcript please be corrected?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The witness actually said May, but the document says July. The witness said May, he probably just misspoke. I won't quibble about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The document says July; doesn't it Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact of the matter is, the bottom line is some people, some soldiers from the Central Bosnia Operative Zone were being sent to Croatia to train.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From this document it is clear that these were individuals and groups who went for such training, as is stated in this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's then turn to the actual training of recruits. Now, the individuals that were taken into the HVO, many of those men had already done national service in the JNA; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then there were those that were brought into the HVO who had not served in the JNA; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, these young men volunteered, as did the others. They voluntarily joined the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we established this morning, Brigadier, that they were all drafted. I mean, there was conscription and everybody was drafted as a result of the 3 July, 1992 edict that Blaskic put in effect the next day; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Objection, that is what the Prosecutor said, the witness never said that. The witness said there was a legal basis, he said that Blaskic gave the order, but that the situation on the ground differed, so that voluntariness remained the basic principle. Now the Prosecutor is putting into the witness's mouth what he believes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the record can speak for itself, we'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn our attention to Exhibit 456/79.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: On what subject, Mr. Prosecutor, still the same subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The same subject, Mr. President, still on the training of recruits issue. It should be an order of 20 September, 1992, Mr. Dubuisson. That's not it. This is it. I'm sorry, it should be Exhibit 456/79.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let us take a look -- INTERPRETER: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, take a look at Exhibit 456/79. It, again, is an order that is signed by the accused, dated 20 September, 1992. Brigadier, I'll read the preparatory paragraph and then move down to paragraph number 3. "Tasks of the Central Bosnia HVO command headquarters. On the basis of a clear need for a more expeditious work of an improved quality in September 1992, the following essential tasks are to be carried out by the appointed time and the person responsible for the task. 3. The training of new recruits who have not served in the Yugoslav army is to be basic and specific; recruit all able-bodied men over 18." The person responsible for this task was head of operations and training. Brigadier, you did not come to the headquarters until the 1st, or approximately the 1st of November, 1992, and I take it that your predecessor was responsible for that. But are you familiar with this document, sir, and the order to train new recruits who have not served in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document was signed by General Blaskic. I recognise his signature. The document was issued before I joined the command of the Operative Zone, but as far as I know this activity that is ordered under point three was not carried out in that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, an entire plan for the training of recruits was set out by General Petkovic of the HVO in September of 1992; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that plan and programme of training. I don't know exactly when it was issued. But I was speaking about the conditions under which we were working and living in the Operative Zone. As far as I can recall, this task in the area of the Lasva Valley, that is the Vitez, Busovaca, Novi Travnik enclave and a part of the Travnik area, I shall try and be precise. We partly carried it out in September 1993, a part of this order, because we were short of men on the front. At that time we did carry out what is referred to in point three under improvised conditions, where we put up recruits in the elementary school in Nova Bila. I only recall those activities in that period of time in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let me show you, again, Exhibit 456/107, another document that comes from Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you prefer us to have a break now, because I see that there is some difficulty in finding the document? Mr. Dubuisson, have you found it? Very well, we will have a break immediately after we examine this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine, Judge, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, you said in the prior exhibit, in the order of 20 September, 1992, that the training of recruits was not completed; and we have before us an Exhibit 456/107, a packet communication from General Blaskic as of the 19th of November, 1992. It has a rather elaborate timed training schedule that runs from 0600, getting up in the morning, to callisthenics, personal hygiene, inspection, one training period, two training periods, three training periods, four training periods, five training periods, break for lunch, again, we train again, in the afternoon after lunch, and then the seventh training period and recess before taps. Read the bottom part, and keep in mind your comment about training in barracks. "This daily schedule to apply to all barracks, buildings where members of the armed forces are accommodated in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and barrack commanders shall adhere to the above schedule." Now, would you agree with me, Brigadier, that for a place where no training is going on, this is a pretty elaborate schedule?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is an elaborate schedule. As far as I recall, this was copied from the regulations booklet of the former Yugoslav People's Army, and this kind of a timetable exists in any organised army. That was what we sought to achieve, and we addressed such a document to our subordinates, so that if they should find themselves in such a situation they would know how to behave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean the bottom line, Brigadier, is that Blaskic ordered that training be done, and training was being done; isn't that a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Training was not done as ordered. I said when, under what conditions and in what time period such training was done with recruits in the Lasva Valley, or rather the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you. If it's convenient for the Court to take a break at this time, if it's convenient?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, we will resume work at a quarter past 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you. We move to another exhibit. If I could hand this to the usher. Again, Mr. President, there is no French translation yet on this document, but we will provide it. It is a multi-page document, Mr. President, so it might be difficult to put on the ELMO. Maybe we could just put the cover sheet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 484, 484A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, are you familiar with this training manual that was signed on the cover by General Milivoj Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen this kind of plan and programme in the command of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we just go through it, and we need not read this whole matter, this is a rather extensive 22-day period, rather extensive programme for a 22-day period for recruits in the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that can be seen from this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the type of training that was being contemplated by Colonel Blaskic in the previous exhibit where we had this training schedule running from 6.00 in the morning until 21.00 hours in the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we link the document we saw a moment ago to this one, I would not be able to say that they are directly linked. But if we were to compare the schedules then we would see here in items one and two, it says eight hours daily, two hours in the morning, two hours in the afternoon. So these match and they could be linked together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, now this basic training that was employed by Blaskic, and that was set out by General Petkovic -- take a look through this, it has a variety of aspects of training for new recruits, doesn't it? Some in firearms, some in mortars, tactical training, infantry weapons, medical care, engineering, physical exercise, et cetera. It's a rather broad range of subjects, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I should like to spend a little time on this document and try to explain the previous document. In the HVO, this programme did exist. Also, there were orders. We saw the number of orders issued by the Commander of the Operative Zone regarding organisation, the prevention of arbitrary behaviour. As many orders were issued by the Commander of the Operative Zone in connection with the implementation of this programme. Therefore, the documents existed both at the level of the main headquarters and the command of the Operative Zone. We wanted to organise the army and to do everything in the best possible way but the situation on the ground was different. For that reason we have quite a number of orders by General Blaskic, within a short period of time, ordering the execution of certain actions. We saw those orders with regard to organisation. We are now seeing them in relation to training. Then there were other documents concerning crime and other such occurrences. General Blaskic, as a professional military man, knew what an army meant and how an army is established. He wanted to implement the regulations that we had but the situation on the ground was a different matter and it was not possible to put into effect the things in the way we wanted or in the way ordered by the Commander of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you said, Brigadier --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, Brigadier, that you were familiar with this document and that you'd seen it in the Operative Zone headquarters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this document and I saw it in the command of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw it during the time that you were in charge of training; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I joined the Operative Zone headquarters, I cannot remember exactly when this programme reached us, the programme which we were assigned to carry out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, look through this document, Brigadier. Is there any notation or comment in this document that calls for the training of recruits in the Laws and Customs of War in the Geneva Conventions? There isn't, is there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in this document, in this pile of pages that I have, I see no mention of that subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in addition to this training manual, as the head of training in the headquarters, you were also familiar with the armed forces instruction manual issued by the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, the HVO defence department, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several handbooks. Could I please see the handbook and the date? A handbook that came from the main headquarters in '93 and '94, there were several such handbooks, so I don't know exactly which one you're referring to. If I could see it, I would be able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Absolutely, Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a handbook dated Mostar, 1992. It is a rather extensive armed forces manual. We have simply translated the index and we're unable to give a translation for all of the BCS going into French and English. It's just too extensive, given the work going in the translation section at this point.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document 485, 485A for the translation of the index.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, you mentioned that there --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could we have one, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, is there not another one? Here's another one. Here, you can put this on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, you mentioned that there were several manuals that were issued by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, since the time of the establishment of the HVO, which is, well, April '92 until its transformation along with the BH army into the federation army, there were several manuals which we were supposed to use and which we did use in training of our units. When you said that you had this handbook, this is what I wanted to have in order to be able to specifically answer your questions in that regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you just noted that this was a handbook that was used in the training of your personnel, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This handbook, in this volume, there are contained several parts, one would be the training manual of the armed forces. Let me see if there are other enclosures here. Mr. President, Your Honours, this is just one portion of the entire handbook which was entitled, "The General Rules of the Armed Forces." One would be the rules, the training handbook. This would have been the entire volume and this is just one portion of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would know better than I, Brigadier, how many other volumes are there in addition to this volume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The entire handbook would be a three part thing. One is the Rules of Service. One would be the Training and then one would be the Rules and one would be the Discipline Rules. So this portion that has been enclosed here is the training manual. This would be the drill, but not the tactical. In other words, this would be how to address your superior, how to salute. This is what was regulated in the portion of the handbook that we have in front of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The actual armed forces instruction manual, of which this is a part, is somewhat extensive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is entitled, "The General Rules of Service in the Armed Forces." It actually has four parts: One would be the General Rules of Service; one would be the Training Manual; one would be the Ritual and one would be the Discipline.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is just simply one of four volumes is all I am trying to get at. There are three other volumes in addition to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, was this training manual adopted from the Republic of Croatia? Take a look at the first paragraph after the index. Paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say whether it was taken over or not. The author of this would know the best. That is the author of this instruction manual. But a large part of its contents has been taken over from the JNA. It was linguistically adjusted to the Croatian way of speaking. We have to realise that this was done during the war and you did not have expert teams which would have changed things around at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Read that first sentence in paragraph 1, Brigadier. If we could put it on the ELMO in the BCS. This paragraph here. No, right here. That's it. So the folks in the translation booth can read it. Do you see that okay? Can you read that, Brigadier, that first sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Chapter 1, General Provisions: 1. "This training manual regulates instructions and actions of individuals and the following units: squads, platoons, companies and battalions on land which should be unified for the entire Croatian army. The units of different branches and arms and services which are not covered by this instruction manual shall act according to the provisions of this instruction manual with respect to the real conditions, equipment and weapons available."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Brigadier, in addition to the training recruits, and in addition to this manual, Blaskic issued order for specialised training even to special purpose units, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to see such a document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exhibit 456/2. We'll focus on paragraph 3 of that document. Now, Brigadier, this is a document dated the 26th of September, 1992, 12.00 hours from the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. It was signed by Colonel Blaskic, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll repeat myself. This is a document of the 26th of September, 1992, at 12.00 hours from the Central Bosnia Operative Zone and it was, in fact, signed by Colonel Blaskic with his seal. Is that right, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is General Blaskic's signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's just read it briefly. It's an order to form units for assault operations. "Further to Order No. 012173/92, dated 21 September, 1992, of the general staff and in order to ensure the full and timely execution of tasks and form special units for combat operations, as well as, intervention in areas under threat, I hereby issue the following order:" He gives orders to the municipal staff on the structure. But look at No. 3, because that deals with the subject we've been discussing on training. "Initiate, immediately, drills and training for the special purpose units, PPN, for assault operations and train the PPN to platoon level while concentrating on anti-tank groups, sniper groups, groups for destroying firing points, bomb points, groups for liquidation using cold steel" -- and I believe steel is spelled incorrectly in the English -- "Groups for clearing trenches and communication trenches" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We're not getting the translation into French. It would be best if the document could be placed correctly on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just dealing with that No. 3. I'll read it again: "Initiate, immediately, drills and training for the special purposes unit, PPN, for assault operations. Train the PPN to platoon levels while concentrating on anti-tank groups, sniper groups, groups for destroying firing points, bombing groups, groups for liquidation using cold steel, groups for clearing trenches and communications trenches, reconnaissance of enemy deployment." Now that's very specific training, is it not, Brigadier, being set out on the 26th of September, 1992, by Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The training programme was not elaborated here. This is just to point out what these people should be trained in. Mr. President, I would like to point out the date when this document was drafted and the situation which we had in Central Bosnia. This was 26 September, 1992. In the area of Zepce, Jajce, Novi Travnik, Kiseljak, Travnik, Bugojno municipalities, there were very strong attacks being carried out by the Bosnian Serb army. As I said, we did not have organised forces at that time and we had a need. We had people at the line of defence and we did not have solutions as to what to do if those lines would fall, how we would prevent a further advance of the Bosnian Serb army. These are the reasons why the commander who was in charge of the defence of a particular line had an idea and this is as early as 1992, how to most efficiently counter that pressure. This is why he issued such an order. I know that because of the situation and conditions on the ground which were similar to what I have said with respect to organisation and training, was not implemented. So the forces which have been ordered here, we never had in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, suffice to say, based on what we've seen this afternoon, you'll agree with me that on the 20th of September, Colonel Blaskic issued orders on training of new recruits that we saw in Exhibit 456/79 and on the 26th of September, he issued an order to train special purpose units and I might add that in Point 2, he required experienced and discipline soldiers. We discussed Exhibit 456/107, 19th November, 1992, the rather extensive training schedule in barracks of recruits. Now would you agree with me that that is a somewhat extensive training schedule and you were the chief training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can agree with you on only the following: That these documents were drafted and signed by the commander of the Operative Zone at the time which is indicated. I cannot agree with you about the practice of implementing them. You saw how many orders General Blaskic issued with respect to training. Within a month or so we have as many as three; but we could not implement them on the ground, due to the circumstances which I explained. Also, as far as the kind of work that we were able to carry out, these were only with the soldiers which we had with the BH army in Travnik and in the barracks in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, after November the 1st, or the 1st of November, 1992, when you took over the operations and training section, did you begin to train HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under conditions which I inherited when I started, the situation changed. Jajce had fallen, and we fought alongside the BH army troops in order to prevent the breakthrough of the Bosnian Serb army in the Travnik municipality. We had a similar situation in the Zepce municipality. When I arrived in the Operative Zone command, the war was spreading and the conditions which were prevailing in July and August, and even April, were completely obsolete and we did not take any, we did not consider them anymore, because the situation had changed. I'm talking about the situation on the ground, and the document speaks about what the commander wanted to do and what his intention was with respect to the organisation of the units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe you didn't understand my question, Brigadier. When you took over on 1 November, 1993, did you supervise or were you involved in training of HVO soldiers? You?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I took over as department head, I was mostly involved in the lines of defence and the situation there. I did not have the time or opportunity to conduct or implement training programmes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, you took over in 1 November, 1992, I think, I misspoke and said 1993. Let me show you a document, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is 486, 486A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, take a look at this document, Brigadier. Is that your signature on this document? Is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not my signature. This was signed by someone else on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was signed on your behalf. Who signed it on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you will allow me, let me just review the contents and I may be able to draw a conclusion. This was signed by the operations duty officer, so, it could have been my assistant. I don't know who it was on the 23rd of November, 1992. However, if you want an answer as to whether there was training on the artillery crews, yes, the crews trained on the firing positions and this training was conducted by the artillery chief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's read this, Brigadier. 23rd of November 1992, it goes to the assistant for logistics, Central Bosnia Operative Zone, I believe it's a gentleman you discussed previously, Franjo Sliskovic. Subject is securing devices for Zis gun, Z-I-S. "It is necessary to urgently secure sighting devices for a Zis gun, as well as binoculars. Check with Novi Travnik logistics if Bratstvo has them," in handwriting, "sighting devices from another is also possible. The above-mentioned sighting devices are needed for the training of newly formed crews." So, crews were, in fact, being trained during this period of time; isn't that right, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, regarding this specific Zis gun, we only had two Zis guns in the entire Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, you were doing training, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did work on training. These two Zis guns were a part of the artillery battery, and the training for these artillery pieces and command were all -- the commander of the artillery was in charge of this training.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, when you told us several minutes ago that you were not involved in training during this time period, what you told this Court was not accurate; was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not agree with what you said. I said that the focus of my work, when I arrived at the Operative Zone command, was the lines of defence because those were the needs of the situation. In this time period, I mostly worked on that, obviously with all other work at the Operative Zone command. There was no major training, such as would have been needed had we had conditions. That I did not do, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, did the training in the Central Bosnian Operative Zone continue even until the outbreak of hostilities with the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The basic training which was conducted in the units in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone was the handling of small arms. If you were in infantry, you had to learn how to use the infantry weapons. If you had to be trained to use an artillery piece, then other members of the crew would train this new soldier while they were in a firing position. Other portions of the training, such as was defined here in this instruction manual, according to the plans that existed, we did not carry out such training, with respect to all the hours and all the elements and everything else which is spelled out in this programme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, after the conflict between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO in early January -- excuse me, late January and early February of 1992, there was a cease-fire that was signed on the 13th of February, 1993. I think there was a series of documents presented by the Defence on that subject; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, you're asking me about the date of the signing of a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we will agree those documents were in fact signed on the 13th of February of 1993 between Enver Hadzihasanovic and Colonel Blaskic. After the conflict between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO was completed in February, did Blaskic order additional training for HVO troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not order additional training, but in 1993 the only organised training which we conducted was with a group of new recruits in the Nova Bila elementary school. These would be the new recruits, and this is under conditions which we had and with equipment which we had. This training mostly consisted in handling small arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take a look at Exhibit 456/15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, in the transcript apparently you said "after the conflict between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO was completed in February."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What is meant by "a conflict being completed"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge Riad, documents that were submitted both by the Defence, through Brigadier Marin, and also with Colonel Remi Landry, who was then with ECMM, Canadian armed forces, the conflict in the Busovaca area between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO took place late January early February. A series of documents ordering a cease-fire and various measures to be taken was signed on the 13th of February, 1993, by the accused, as well as General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What is the meaning of "completed"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It may be inaccurate, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I wanted to know when the conflict is completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Maybe it was just a slow boil. In any event, those documents are signed on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, take a look at this document, it is a two-page document dated the 13th of February, 1993, same day these agreements are signed. I believe this is, again, a packet communication system; is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at the lower left-hand corner; who wrote this document? Whose initials are down in the lower left-hand corner? SM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: SM, those are my initials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those are yours, okay. You were the drafter of this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of an assignment given to me by the commander of the Operative Zone, I drafted this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
