utterances.text: Naturally, I wouldn't infer anything else, Brigadier. I just want to read you some subjects in this document, and it goes to a variety of units, and it says: "Organisational order for further action. Due to the very extreme activities by the enemy, and shortcomings in the command and the control of the HVO units, and in order to raise the level of combat readiness, I hereby," let's turn our attention to number 4 in a list of 12 paragraphs: It says, "Carry out additional training and live firing practice for sniper groups from all units of the Central Bosnian Operative Zone. Person responsible for the task, assistant for ONP in the unit. Monitoring and supervision will be carried out by the ONP assistant, Central Bosnian Operative Zone, deadline 20 February, 1993." Now, Brigadier, I asked you several minutes ago whether or not Blaskic ordered additional training after the conflict was over in mid-February, between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the HVO, and you said no. Do you want to change that answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I should like to give my answer to this document and to clarify something. The document was drafted on the 13th of February, 1993. True, at the time, there was a cessation of hostilities between the HVO and the BH army. When I made my presentation and answered questions by Mr. Nobilo, I kept underlining the fact that we, or that is the HVO, from April 1992, had a defence line facing the army of Republika Srpska, constantly, until June 1993 when units of the BH army, in the area of Travnik and Novi Travnik, attacked HVO units from behind units that were facing the Bosnian Serbs. After the cease-fire was signed, which is linked to the conflict in Busovaca, the activities of the Republika Srpska armies along the defence lines held by the HVO were intensified, and according to our estimates there was a danger of the Bosnian Serb army taking advantage of the conflicts and misunderstandings between the BH army and the HVO to attack our defence lines. This order went to all HVO units which held defence lines towards the Bosnian Serbs. So, this order was linked exclusively to the organisation of a quality defence against the Bosnian Serbs. That is the only answer I can give.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, did Blaskic, or did he not, order additional sniper training in this order on the 13th of February, that you drafted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The question was already asked, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question; did the additional sniper training take place pursuant to Blaskic's order on the 13th of February?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regarding the training of snipers, I know that instructors for sniper fire did not exist in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, so that we couldn't implement sniper training in the full sense of the word. As an officer specialising in training, you need special instructors to provide quality training and special devices and conditions in order to train people for the use of such devices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know a man by the name of Vlado Ilic, also known as Golden Eye, and was he a trained sniper who was in the Vitez area under Blaskic's command, and was he awarded, or given an award by President Boban for killing 72 people? Are you familiar with this man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know Mr. Vlado Ilic. You said that he was from Vitez; didn't you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a sniper in the Viteska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man who had the nickname of Golden Eye, in the Vitez area, who was a sniper for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know any such man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know any instance when a sniper for the HVO, in the Vitez area, was given an award by Mate Boban for killing 72 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such award, nor of any such person. Could you perhaps tell me when this award was given because after the Washington Accords, I was transferred to the command in Tomislavgrad, and I spent two years there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It could very well be, Brigadier, that that award was given after the Washington Accords. On the sniper fire, did the HVO have snipers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO did not have organised snipers. I should like to try and explain what snipers are in the war that was waged in Bosnia-Herzegovina, both on the side of the BH army units and the HVO. The HVO, as far as I know, the soldiers on the front-lines used, as snipers, hunting carbines with optical sights, and they also used improvised M48 rifles with sights. This is an improvisation. I do not know, at least, I'm not familiar with whether anyone had an original real military sniper rifle. These kind of snipers that I have referred to were used on the defence lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I see the series of exhibits beginning in 80, and I believe in Exhibit 80 we have a weapon in that regard. Can I see that? Prosecutor's Exhibit 80. I take that back, Mr. Dubuisson, it's Exhibit 82.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, can I just see those? Would you show these two photographs to the Brigadier and put them on the ELMO? For the record, Mr. Usher, what is the record of the photograph we have on the ELMO. THE USHER: 82/10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could put 82/10 on the ELMO first and move the photograph up just a bit to put the rifle --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see that rifle, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of rifle is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a sniper rifle, 12.7 millimetres, which is used to neutralise enemy fortifications, because of its calibre size at larger distances. I can't tell you what the range is exactly, but I think it is greater than that of regular sniper rifles. Talking about snipers, I have just recalled a statement made by General Blaskic to UNPROFOR. I was reminded by these photographs, in which HVO soldiers are simply showing off what kind of weapons they have. They know that an UNPROFOR officer came to see General Blaskic and reproach him about this, and he literally said, "Any soldier that you see carrying a sniper rifle in the street, feel free to seize it from him." I remember that very well, because this was recounted in our command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, we will just put the other photograph on the ELMO so we have an idea what we're talking about, and the number on that photograph? THE USHER: 82/9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, that is the same photograph of the sniper rifle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we move away from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just want to know who would feel free to seize him? It says if you find somebody carrying a sniper, feel free to seize him. The UNPROFOR officer would seize the sniper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Blaskic, in response to complaints by UNPROFOR, that along the roads being used by UNPROFOR and HVO members, that they had seen HVO members showing off with these weapons, because this is a weapon with strong fire power. General Blaskic prohibited it. I think there is an order to that effect and to prove to UNPROFOR that he doesn't support the use of such weapons, he said, "Seize those weapons from them and tell me who had them." It was in that context that this statement was recounted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, but was it within the authority of UNPROFOR to seize arms of HVO? Did they have this authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the details regarding the mission and authority of UNPROFOR in Central Bosnia, whether they had the authority to seize such weapons and under which conditions. Maybe if they were, personally, in jeopardy, but I can't say that with any precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just finishing up on this particular document that you wrote, Brigadier, on the 13th of February, there were, in fact, sniper groups in all of the units within the Central Bosnian Operative Zone; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. Organised sniper groups did not exist, because there was no one to train them, to act as organised sniper groups. I know a little from literature about sniper training, the training in pairs, in combination and so on. If in a unit you had two men with sniper rifles that I have mentioned, the improvised kind that I described, then this cannot be described as a sniper group. A sniper group must be a well-trained group who are familiar with the tactics, the technical characteristics, the use of such weapons in all weather conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the fact is, of course, Brigadier, that General Blaskic himself said to carry out additional training for sniper groups from all units in the Central Bosnian Operative Zone. Now, the training of these recruits and the training of personnel continued throughout the war in Central Bosnia; didn't it, up until the Washington Accords?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Talking about the training of recruits, I know that in the Lasva Valley, we trained recruits. I think it was the end of August '93 or September '93 in the facility, that is the school at Bila, which we used as a barracks. Because we were surrounded and isolated from Kiseljak and Zepce, I do not know whether they engaged in any training under the conditions in which they were living. We carried out this training because in the war of '93, we had very high casualties. We were lacking men on the front-lines and we had to train young men over 18 as quickly as possible. I can't tell you how many of them there were to assist and reinforce the front-lines. Let me give you an example of the shortage of men. When I went to the Viteska Brigade in December 1993, after an attack by BiH army units in Busancavo Selo (phoen), when we had 70 dead in one night, we were lacking men. As a member of that command, I had to spend three hours, during the night, in the trenches and then go on with my regular duties the next day because we were lacking men. Therefore, even though we didn't have the necessary conditions for quality training of recruits, we decided, at least, to train these young men how to hold a rifle, how to use it, so that they could be used on less dangerous positions that were less exposed to attacks by BH army forces, so that they would be able to participate in the defence. Those were the conditions under which, in the Lasva Valley in '93, we trained recruits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Mr. President. If I could show you and put on the ELMO, Prosecutor's Exhibit 433/8. By way of refreshing the Court, Mr. President, Your Honours, this was a photograph that was taken by then, Captain Lee Whitworth of the Prince of Wales Regiment of Yorkshire, and I believe late summer, early fall of 1993, but it was certainly during the Prince of Wales own tour. That's it. Brigadier, this is a photograph taken by a British battalion officer in late summer, early fall of 1993 of what he testified are HVO recruits training in the streets in and around Vitez. Is this photograph accurate to portray the type of training these recruits were doing in and around the streets of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Recruits were not trained in Vitez, they were trained in Nova Bila. But this is quite close. The distance is not great between Nova Bila and Vitez. I cannot recognise whether these are recruits. But from what can be seen on this photograph, we see that the recruits are being trained too much in a military fashion. We had this kind of training in the exercise manual of the armed forces and this is not the training for combat. The fundamental focus of training was to teach recruits to use infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fundamental training for recruits is the use of infantry weapons, working together, drilling together and marching together and that's what's going on in this photograph, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In peacetime conditions, the fundamental training of recruits in an organised army is far more complex. I said under what conditions we were training recruits in Nova Bila. The conditions were such that in September, the HVO in Vitez had more than 400 dead in Travnik, more than 300 in Busovaca, about 250 and so on. So the conditions were such that we didn't have the manpower to hold defence lines and we were lacking men. That is why out of necessity we opted to take this step. This training was incomplete and these young men were certainly not trained for adequate use in combat operations. May I draw your attention to this relief, this model? Mr. President, you see the green flags on this model. You see that we were surrounded and it was under such conditions of siege that we were carrying out this training. When any person who is capable of carrying a weapon had to be used for defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could just move that back from the Brigadier. Before we leave this area, though, Brigadier, the bottom line is you were doing training, isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It cannot be said that there was no training. It was reduced to a minimum and exclusively to meet fundamental, elementary needs for the soldier to be able to correctly behave while holding defence lines. A proper organisation of training, such as you would have under peacetime, did not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: He has not asked you this question. He has asked you whether the bottom line is that you were doing training. Now, that is not answered by a statement to the effect that such training as was being done was minimal. Could you please answer the Prosecutor's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we carried out the minimal and most essential training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am about to go into a somewhat lengthy area. I am glad to begin. I am glad to go on. I would just like to know for the Court's purposes, if the Court would like me to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We could stop now, although we have a few minutes left. What subject did you want to take up?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We're going to discuss the testimony that was -- or the subject raised by Judge Riad, specifically, on the power to appoint and dismiss commanders and I believe several days ago, Judge Riad asked a specific question in that regard. We have somewhat lengthy questions on that subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, did you want to say something? What did you want to speak about?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, just to say, Mr. President, it would be helpful if we could have some idea of when to have the next witness on hand. Right now we have no idea if a witness may be needed on Friday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday of next week. If there could be some information in that regard, it would help us use the Court time efficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good question, but I think it depends. First of all, it depends on the Prosecutor when he finishes, then it depends on you because you have a re-examination; right? Then there are the questions that the Judges want to ask. So I really can't answer you. Perhaps the Prosecutor, who, for the time being, is holding the key to his own cross-examination could tell us when he will finish, or is it difficult to say? The time has to remain a bit fluid. Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think at this point, Mr. President, it has to remain somewhat fluid. I want to move through this as expeditiously, but these are very significant areas that were brought out by the defence in numerous documents that need to be addressed. I do not want to prolong this any more than I have to, but the trial team has tried to cut this down as much as possible and I will move as quickly as possible. I simply, at this point, can't give a specific time. I would venture to say that given the questions that remain for the Brigadier and that remain for re-direct examination and for the questions by the Judges, I don't think we will have another witness this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to speak with my colleagues because the Judges have, in my opinion, the responsibility to set limits, both for the examination-in-chief and for the cross-examination and not allow for time to remain just completely vague. This refers to the Defence in this case, but I would like to consult with my colleagues about this. The Judges are very concerned about the time being taken for this testimony, but at the same time they are aware of the importance of the testimony. They have decided that the Prosecution should not take more time than was taken by the Defence for the presentation of its evidence. That would be the limit. As I said, the Prosecution should not exceed the total time that the Defence used for the examination-in-chief, for the cross-examination. Secondly, that's the maximum amount of time. The Judges recommend that the Prosecutor try as best he can to remain on, short of the line. That is, to try to finish before that deadline. How many half days were used by the Defence? I turn to the Registrar, he can tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Calendar days, it was six and a half days and hearing days from five -- there were four and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, the Judges are requesting that the cross-examination not exceed -- how did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Four and a half days of hearing time. That is 320 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 320 minutes. As much as possible, Mr. Prosecutor, the Judges would like for you to finish sooner. This is a recommendation that they are making. Then, we will ask the Defence, in view of what the substance of this cross-examination will have been, to set the amount of time that it plans to take. Last point, if for exceptional reasons, you were to exceed the amount of time given to you, the time, of course, would not be counted as the general Defence time. That's what we can say insofar as setting the day for the probable return of the witness to his home. Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President. I understand the parameters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, you heard that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I did, Mr. President. If there is some way to fashion some incentive for, quite frankly, either party not to exceed time spent by the participant that conducted the direct examination, in other words, if perhaps time spent over that time period came out of the amount of time allotted to the rebuttal case, some incentive, because otherwise I am a little concerned there is no incentive to end. Although it wouldn't be counted against the Defence, the Prosecutor might choose to go on for eight days, because it's not coming out of his time. I just mention that as something, food for thought, as we say in my language. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are all aware of the fact that there is a problem, but for the time being we cannot settle it in any other way from the way that we did. Of course, I call to the Prosecutor's attention for the time being, he is using Defence time. Therefore, we're recommending, and I am doing it, as well as I am asking you as much as you can, to simplify your questions. This is an important witness and I think for the time being we cannot say anything further. We will resume the hearing tomorrow morning at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 5.28 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of October, 1998, at 10.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
